title: Vitamin C facilitates direct cardiac reprogramming by inhibiting reactive oxygen species

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, paragraph 1: SAHA/VPA claim citing [26]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [26] is Vaseghi et al. 2016, 'Generation of an inducible fibroblast cell line for studying direct cardiac reprogramming' — a cell-line methods paper, not an HDAC-inhibitor paper. The SAHA/VPA-hiPSC claim should cite [22] Huangfu et al. 2008. [26] is correctly cited in the Methods for the Doxy-inducible system, creating internal inconsistency with its Discussion usage.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, paragraph 1: 5-AZA claim citing [35]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [35] is Mizuguchi et al. 2017, 'Low dose resveratrol ameliorates mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction and enhances cellular reprogramming' — a resveratrol paper, not a 5-AZA paper. The 5-AZA claim should cite [29] Yoon et al. 2006. [35] is correctly used for resveratrol in the ROS paragraph of the same Discussion, creating internal inconsistency.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, paragraph 1: CHIR 99021 claim citing [29]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [29] is Yoon et al. 2006, a 5-azacytidine/hanging-drop hESC differentiation paper — not a CHIR 99021/Wnt paper. Should cite [24] Lian et al. 2012. The Results section correctly uses [29] to support 5-AZA in the screening list, directly contradicting this Discussion usage.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, paragraph 1: VitC claim citing [24, 25, 36]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: None of the cited references are VitC papers: [24] is Lian 2012 (Wnt/CHIR), [25] is Chen 2011 (rapamycin), [36] is Yusa 2015 (piggyBac transposon review). The VitC claim should cite [19] Cao 2012, [20] Takahashi 2003, and [21] Esteban 2010 — the same references correctly used in the Background.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, paragraph 1: P53 claim citing [28]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [28] is van Ineveld et al. 2020, 'Single-cell resolution three-dimensional imaging of intact organoids' — an imaging protocol paper, not a P53 paper. Should cite [23] Rasmussen et al. 2014. [28] is correctly cited in the Methods for 3D microtissue imaging, creating internal inconsistency.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, paragraph 1: mTOR inhibitor claim citing [30]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [30] is Smits et al. 2012, 'Isolation and differentiation of human cardiomyocyte progenitor cells' — not an mTOR/rapamycin paper. Should cite [25] Chen et al. 2011 (rapamycin enhances iPSC generation). [30] is correctly cited in Results for the CMPC morphology claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, ROS measurement sentence: 'we determined ROS production by measuring DHA level'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Results claim ROS production was determined by 'measuring DHA level', but the Methods state ROS was measured with a DCFDA assay. Dehydroascorbic acid (DHA) is the compound used as the antioxidant-deficient control treatment, not a ROS readout. 'DHA' here is a conflation with 'DCFDA' (the fluorescent probe), producing a direct internal contradiction between the stated measurement and the actual assay described in Methods.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, paragraph 1: VPA chromatin relaxation claim citing [26, 34]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Neither cited reference supports VPA-mediated chromatin relaxation: [26] is Vaseghi 2016 (inducible cell line) and [34] is Cloos et al. 2008 (histone demethylase review). The claim should cite [22] Huangfu 2008. Additionally, [34] is correctly cited for histone demethylases later in the same Discussion.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods, Statistical analysis: 'comparisons were performed with a t-test (non-parametric tests)'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A t-test is by definition a PARAMETRIC test that assumes normally distributed data. Describing it as 'a t-test (non-parametric tests)' is internally contradictory and factually incorrect; the non-parametric counterparts are the Mann-Whitney U test (unpaired) or Wilcoxon signed-rank test (paired). Additionally, every figure legend reports only two-way ANOVA, and no t-test output is reported anywhere in the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract: 'partly dependent of its antioxidant properties'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Grammatical error affecting meaning: 'dependent of' should be 'dependent on'. The same phrase appears correctly as 'dependent on' later in the Results, making the Abstract version an inconsistency within the paper's own wording.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract: 'fibroblasts from human and mice in 2D and 3D model'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Grammar errors affecting precision: 'human and mice' should be 'human and mouse' (adjective form), and '2D and 3D model' should be '2D and 3D models' (plural). The identical phrasing also appears in the Abstract Results paragraph.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction: 'limited to left ventricle assistant devices (LVADs)'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The correct medical term is 'left ventricular assist devices'; 'left ventricle assistant devices' is a terminology error that deviates from standard usage throughout the field and could mislead readers.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion, ROS paragraph: dehydroascorbic acid 'did not affect cardiac reprogramming efficiency or ROS production'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Results section only reports that DHA treatment produced 'no difference in reprogramming efficiency'. No data are presented anywhere showing the effect of DHA on ROS production. The Discussion therefore asserts a result ('or ROS production') that was never reported in the Results — an unsupported claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract/Results/Discussion: characterization of dehydroascorbic acid as 'a structural analog of VitC but lacking antioxidant properties'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Dehydroascorbic acid is not a 'structural analog' of ascorbic acid; it is the two-electron oxidized form of ascorbic acid. Moreover, DHA is transported into cells via GLUT transporters and intracellularly reduced back to ascorbate, so the assertion that it 'lacks antioxidant properties' is a scientifically contested simplification. The paper's central mechanistic argument depends on this characterization.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results screening section / Discussion small-molecule paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims 'We screened seven factors' (SAHA, VPA, 5-AZA, CHIR 99021, VitC, mTOR inhibition, p53 inhibition), but Results report outcomes only for VPA, SAHA, and VitC. No screening results are reported for CHIR 99021, the mTOR inhibitor, or the p53 inhibitor, and 5-AZA is only mentioned in the Discussion. The claim of a complete seven-factor screen is unsupported by the reported data.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results (ROS measurement) vs Abbreviations list: 'DHA' used for both dehydroascorbic acid and apparently the DCFDA fluorescent readout
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Results text reads 'measuring DHA level' to describe ROS quantification, but the Abbreviations section defines 'DHA: Dehydroascorbic acid' — the antioxidant-deficient control compound. The ROS assay is actually DCFDA, and Fig. 6 reports 'DCF/Hoechst ratio'. 'DHA' is ambiguously used for two different meanings within the same paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract: 'We screened seven factors capable of improving direct cardiac reprogramming of both mice and human fibroblasts'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Two problems: (1) 'capable of improving' presupposes the screening outcome before testing; (2) the screening was performed in MEFs only — in human cells (hFCFs) only VitC was tested. The abstract overstates the screening scope as covering both mouse and human fibroblasts.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction: 'Our findings offer a cost-effective, safe, and efficient strategy for generating iCMs'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'Safe' and 'efficient' are not supported by the evidence: the study is entirely in vitro, no in vivo or toxicity data are provided, the authors report no spontaneous beating even with iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte culture media, and VitC at 100 μg/mL actually reduced efficiency below baseline.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, ROS/P53 paragraph: 'indicating that VitC promotes cardiac reprogramming by reducing ROS-induced cell death'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The causal conclusion — that VitC promotes reprogramming specifically 'by reducing ROS-induced cell death' — is presented as an inference but no cell death/apoptosis data are reported anywhere. The P53 expression change is consistent with multiple interpretations, and linking it specifically to ROS-induced cell death is an unmeasured mechanistic leap.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction: garbled advantages sentence mixing 'cell-free approach' with cell-based strategy advantages
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The sentence lists advantages including 'prevention of cell wash-out upon injection due to the presence of fibroblasts' AND 'the cell-free approach, thereby avoiding wash-out upon injection'. The wash-out advantage is asserted twice with incompatible logic, and describing the approach simultaneously as cell-based and 'cell-free' is internally contradictory.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract (Methods) vs Results 'capable of improving' presupposes outcome
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Abstract Methods states 'We screened seven factors capable of improving direct cardiac reprogramming', asserting the outcome before testing. The Introduction says the molecules' ability 'remains uncertain' and Results show two of the seven (VPA, SAHA) actually decreased efficiency, contradicting the 'capable of improving' framing.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results vs Abstract/Discussion: VitC 100 μg/mL toxicity omitted from summary sections
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Results show VitC at 100 μg/mL reduced GFP+ to 22.6% (below the 25% Doxy-alone baseline), a biphasic/toxic effect. The Abstract and Discussion summaries omit this finding entirely while highlighting toxicity of VPA and SAHA. The Discussion does not mention VitC's own inhibitory effect at high concentration.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods vs figure legends: t-test mentioned in Methods but absent from all figure legends
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Methods section states both t-test AND two-way ANOVA were used, yet every figure legend (Figs. 2, 4, 5, 6) reports only 'Data were analyzed with two-way ANOVA' and no t-test output appears anywhere. Which test was applied to which comparison is ambiguous, making the statistical analysis unreproducible.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods RNA-seq criteria: p < 10⁻⁶ + |log2FC| ≥ 0.5 yielding 622 DEGs
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: An extremely stringent raw P-value threshold (10⁻⁶, without multiple-testing correction) paired with a modest fold-change cutoff (|log2FC| ≥ 0.5) yielding 622 DEGs is atypical for small-n (n=3) RNA-seq experiments. While not mathematically impossible without raw data, this combination warrants scrutiny.

predicted_errors.error_location: All figure legends: n=3 per group analyzed with parametric tests (two-way ANOVA)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: All quantitative comparisons rely on n=3 per group with parametric tests. With n=3, variance estimates are unstable and normality/homoscedasticity assumptions are untestable. The contradictory 't-test (non-parametric tests)' phrasing suggests awareness that parametric assumptions may not hold, yet parametric tests were applied. A methodological robustness concern, not a provable error.

summary: This paper was verified exhaustively across four dimensions (text consistency, citation accuracy, statistical methods, and cross-section consistency) using a lenient strictness setting. The verification identified 25 potential issues, of which 12 have high confidence (≥0.85). The most critical findings are: (1) A systematic pattern of 7 citation misnumberings in the first paragraph of the Discussion, where references are attached to claims they do not support (e.g., a piggyBac transposon review [36] cited for VitC cardiac differentiation, 3D organoid imaging protocol [28] cited for p53 reprogramming), with confidence 0.90-0.95 for each. (2) A direct internal contradiction in the Results where ROS production is claimed to be measured 'by measuring DHA level' when the Methods describe a DCFDA assay — DHA (dehydroascorbic acid) is the control compound, not a ROS probe (confidence 0.95). (3) A factual error in the Methods where the t-test is described as 'non-parametric' when it is by definition a parametric test (confidence 0.90). (4) Several grammar/terminology errors that affect precision, including 'dependent of' instead of 'dependent on', 'human and mice' instead of 'human and mouse', and 'left ventricle assistant devices' instead of 'left ventricular assist devices' (confidence 0.85-0.90). The citation errors appear confined to the Discussion paragraph 1 and may represent a reference numbering error introduced during manuscript revision, as the same numbers are used correctly in the Methods and Results sections. The DHA/DCFDA terminology confusion and the statistical methods error require correction. Verdict: NEEDS_CORRECTION.
